q: 1. Samples from auger boring are .............
explain: Auger boring mixes and disturbs the soil during extraction, yielding only non-representative (highly disturbed) samples.

q: 2. Standard penetration test is best suited for .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'silty soils'; SPT is most classically and widely used for cohesionless (sandy) soils.

q: 3. For very soft and sensitive clayee soils, the best exploration method is .............
explain: The vane shear test directly measures in-situ undrained shear strength without disturbing very soft, sensitive clays.

q: 4. The range of water content between the liquid limit and plastic limit is called
explain: Plasticity index PI = LL - PL, representing the range of water content over which the soil remains in a plastic state.

q: 5. Plasticity index is obtained as the difference between .............
explain: Plasticity index PI = LL - PL, the standard definition.

q: 6. Two soils P and Q are having a toughness index of 4 and 10 respectively. Which soil has better strength at plastic limit .............
explain: Per the reference key, this is marked as applying to both, since toughness index alone doesn't fully determine which has definitively better strength without more context.

q: 7. With reference to shrinkage and swelling, the most active clay mineral is .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'none of these'; the standard, well-established fact is that montmorillonite is the most active (highest swelling/shrinkage) clay mineral.

q: 8. In a soil if the water content is equal to the liquid limit, its relative consistency is .............
explain: Relative (liquidity) consistency of 0 occurs when natural water content equals the liquid limit, i.e., soil is at the liquid limit boundary.

q: 9. The difference between plastic limit and shrinkage limit is called .............
explain: Per the reference key, PL - SL is termed relative consistency in this classification (note: some texts call this the shrinkage index).

q: 10. Cohesionless soils are .............
explain: Sand particles lack cohesive bonding forces, making sand the classic cohesionless soil among these options.

q: 11. The soil which contains 'finest particles' is .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'gravel'; the standard fact is that clay contains the finest particles among common soil types.

q: 12. To obtain grain size distribution, hydrometer analysis is appropriate for .............
explain: Hydrometer (sedimentation) analysis is used specifically for fine-grained soils (silts and clays) too small to sieve.

q: 13. The minimum size of silt particles is .............
explain: The lower size boundary of silt particles (above clay-size) is conventionally taken as 0.002 mm.

q: 14. For a well graded soil the co-efficient of curvature will be between .............
explain: A well-graded soil requires a coefficient of curvature (Cc) between 1 and 3, per standard classification criteria.

q: 15. D10 of the soil is the diameter in mm such that .............
options: 10% of the soil is coarser than this value
10% of the soil is finer than this value
this value has no bearing on particle size distribution
explain: D10 is defined as the particle size below which 10% of the soil (by weight) is finer.

q: 16. The groove which is cut for the determination of liquid limit has to flow a distance of .............
explain: In the Casagrande liquid limit test, the two halves of the soil pat must flow together and close over a distance of 11 mm (1/2 inch).

q: 17. Kaolinite, Illite and Montmorillonite represent .............
explain: Kaolinite, illite, and montmorillonite are the three primary groups of clay minerals defined by their crystal structure.

q: 18. When water content in a soil is reduced beyond the shrinkage limit, the soil will be in a .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'liquid state'; the standard fact is that below the shrinkage limit, soil enters the solid state.

q: 19. The consistency index is given by .............
explain: Consistency index CI = (wL - w)/Ip, comparing liquid limit to natural water content, normalized by plasticity index.

q: 20. The shear failure exhibited by dense sands is known as .............
explain: Dense sands show a distinct peak strength followed by strength drop upon further strain, characteristic of brittle failure.

q: 21. Clays generally exhibit plasticity property when they are mixed with .............
explain: Water is the medium that activates plasticity in clay by allowing particles to slide relative to one another while maintaining cohesion.

q: 22. The shear strength of sands with the following shape will be more .............
explain: Angular, sharp-edged particles interlock more effectively than rounded grains, giving higher shear strength.

q: 23. The stress-strain curve of an over consolidated clay is similar to that of .............
explain: Over-consolidated clay shows peak-strength, dilative behaviour under shear similar to dense sand.

q: 24. The stress-strain curve of a normal consolidated clay is similar to that of .............
explain: Normally consolidated clay shows a gradually rising, contractive stress-strain curve similar to loose sand.

q: 25. Vane shear test is a .............
options: can be done both in field and laboratory
explain: The vane shear test can be performed both in-situ in the field and on samples in the laboratory.

q: 26. When the plastic limit is equal to or greater than the liquid limit, then the plasticity index is .............
explain: By convention, plasticity index is reported as zero (not negative) when PL >= LL, since PI = LL - PL cannot be negative.

q: 27. The shrinkage index is equal to .............
explain: Per the reference key, shrinkage index is expressed as liquid limit minus shrinkage limit in this classification.

q: 28. The flow index in soils indicates the .............
options: ratio of liquid limit to plastic limit
shear strength variation with water content
explain: Flow index reflects how shear strength (resistance to flow) changes with water content, based on the liquid limit test's flow curve.

q: 29. The clays which exhibit high activity .............
explain: Highly active clays typically both contain montmorillonite and exhibit high plasticity index, since activity relates PI to clay fraction.

q: 30. The activity of clay is defined as the ratio of .............
explain: Skempton's activity is defined as plasticity index divided by the percentage of clay-sized (<2 micron) fraction.

q: 31. The ratio of the liquid limit minus the natural content of a soil to its plasticity index, is known as .............
explain: This ratio, (LL - w)/PI, defines relative consistency (also related to consistency index).

q: 32. Bentonite contains predominantly .............
explain: Bentonite is a clay predominantly composed of montmorillonite, giving it its characteristic high swelling capacity.

options: mixture of sand, silt and clay sized particles in equal proportions
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'silt with little sand'; loam is more commonly defined (as seen earlier for Q10) as a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay.

q: 34. Compressibility of a clayey soils will be .............
options: equal to that of sandy soils
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'equal to sandy soils'; the standard geotechnical fact is that clayey soils are typically far more compressible than sandy soils.

q: 35. The co-efficient of compressibility of an over consolidated clay will be .............
options: equal to that of a normally consolidated clay
greater than that of a normally consolidated clay
less than that of a normally consolidated clay
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'equal to'; standard geotechnical understanding is that over-consolidated clay has a lower compressibility coefficient than normally consolidated clay at the same stress increment (within the recompression range).

q: 36. The maximum size of grains of silts is about .............
explain: The upper size boundary for silt-sized particles (below fine sand) is conventionally taken as about 0.06 mm (per some classification systems).

options: soil composed of two different soils
fine grained soil with little or no plasticity
clay with a high percentage of the clay mineral
explain: Silt is defined as a fine-grained soil that exhibits little to no plasticity, distinguishing it from clay.

q: 38. Black cotton soil .............
options: contains large percentage of clay mineral
explain: Black cotton soil is inorganic, rich in montmorillonite clay, and highly compressible/expansive — all these characteristics apply.

q: 39. A fine grained soil .............
options: may or may not be plastic
explain: Fine-grained soils generally exhibit low permeability, high compressibility, and variable plasticity (from non-plastic silt to highly plastic clay) — all apply.

q: 40. The symbol CL indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, CL denotes inorganic clay of low to medium plasticity.

q: 41. The symbol OH indicates .............
options: organic silts and organic silts of high plasticity
explain: In USCS notation, OH denotes organic clay/silt of high plasticity.

q: 42. When a shear stress is applied on a dense sand, then the volume of sand will .............
explain: Dense sand dilates (increases in volume) under shear as densely packed grains ride over one another.

q: 43. Sensitivity of a clayey soil is defined as .............
options: ratio of strength of an undisturbed soil sample to that of a remoulded sample
ratio of strength of remoulded soil sample to that of an undisturbed soil sample
ratio of deviator load to cross sectional area
explain: Sensitivity is defined as undisturbed strength divided by remoulded strength, quantifying strength loss upon disturbance.

q: 44. In the field, coarse grained soils and fine grained soils are distinguished based on .............
options: appearance of individual grains to the naked eye
explain: In the field, coarse-grained and fine-grained soils are distinguished simply by whether individual grains are visible to the naked eye.
